analysis.one_liner: Raises the corporate tax rate to fund safe, affordable public water and sewer service nationwide.
analysis.headline: Backed by 100 House Democrats, the bill was sent to six committees and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a dedicated federal trust fund for water and sewer infrastructure, paid for by raising the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 24.5% and capped at roughly $35 billion a year. The money would flow to fixing and replacing water pipes, removing lead service lines, treating PFAS contamination, upgrading school drinking water, funding tribal and border-community water systems, and training workers for water-utility jobs. It favors publicly owned water systems: it would let cities buy privately owned water utilities even over the owner's objection, and it would bar federal loan funds from subsidizing water projects that mainly serve new suburban subdivisions. It also requires that funded construction use union project labor agreements where practicable.
analysis.who_benefits: Households facing high water bills or shut-offs for unpaid charges, the estimated millions of homes with lead service lines, communities dealing with PFAS-contaminated water, schools, tribal communities, border colonias, and low-income workers trained into water-utility careers. Unionized construction trades gain steady federally funded work.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households with lead pipes, PFAS, or unaffordable water bills

how_it_helps.text: Creates a dedicated trust fund, without annual reappropriation, capped at the larger of $35 billion a year or one-twentieth of EPA's 20-year water infrastructure need, and funded entirely by a corporate tax increase from 21% to 24.5%.

Splits the money between the clean water and drinking water state revolving loan funds (42% each), with the rest for pollution-control grants, tribal sanitation facilities through the Indian Health Service (3%), household wells, border colonias, and water-operator job training.
Requires states to use at least 50% of loan funds for additional subsidization, effectively grants or loan forgiveness rather than loans, prioritizing disadvantaged communities.

Provides grants to property owners to replace lead service lines, and funding for public water systems to upgrade treatment plants or switch water sources due to PFAS contamination, plus filtration systems for contaminated household wells.
Expands the school drinking water grant program from $5 million to $1.05 billion a year to make school fountains, coolers, and bottle-filling stations lead-free.

Lets municipalities purchase privately owned treatment works and community water systems from a willing or unwilling seller, and directs revolving funds toward publicly owned, operated, and managed water systems.
Funds water and wastewater operator job training, prioritizing low-income residents, communities of color, and tribal communities for at least half the grants.
Requires states to permit and, to the maximum extent practicable, require project labor agreements on construction funded through the revolving funds, and preserves prevailing-wage requirements.

Directs EPA to study water affordability nationwide, water shut-offs, tax liens and foreclosures from unpaid water bills, and discrimination by water providers and state funding administrators, with a report to Congress within a year.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations pay the higher 24.5% corporate tax rate. Investor-owned water utilities face possible purchase through eminent domain. Federal loan funds would be cut off from new suburban development projects that primarily benefit new communities.

drawbacks.text: Raising the corporate rate to 24.5% increases the cost of domestic corporate investment; critics of corporate tax increases argue the cost eventually lands partly on workers and consumers through lower wages and higher prices.

Allowing purchase of privately owned water utilities from an unwilling seller uses eminent domain to transfer private property to public ownership, which raises property-rights objections and could deter private investment in water systems.

Barring state revolving fund assistance for projects that provide substantial direct benefits to new communities, except advanced decentralized wastewater systems, would deny subsidized financing for the sewer and water extensions new housing developments need.
The bill commits tens of billions of dollars a year in mandatory spending outside the normal annual appropriations process, which reduces congressional oversight of how the money is spent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: EPA's own assessments put the 20-year national water infrastructure need in the hundreds of billions of dollars, far beyond current appropriations, and lead pipes and PFAS in drinking water are direct health hazards, so the case for large dedicated funding is strong. The corporate tax increase is a modest rate rise (3.5 points) but broad-based. The most contested design choices are the eminent-domain purchases of private utilities and the ban on subsidizing new-development projects; the bill never advanced far enough for those to be tested or amended.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to six House committees when introduced in March 2023; none of them took it up beyond sending it to subcommittees, and it died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the bill on March 22, 2023, with 64 original cosponsors.
It was referred to six committees: Transportation and Infrastructure, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Agriculture, Natural Resources, and Education and the Workforce.

Within weeks it was sent to subcommittees on Water Resources and Environment, Environment Manufacturing and Critical Materials, and Commodity Markets Digital Assets and Rural Development, and no committee ever reported it out.
It drew 100 cosponsors, every one of them a Democrat, and no Republican.
The House took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Investor-owned water utilities and corporations that would have paid the higher tax rate are better off because the bill never moved; households with lead pipes, PFAS contamination, or unaffordable water bills gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private water utilities and corporate taxpayers

industries.note: The bill would let municipalities buy privately owned water and sewer systems from a willing or unwilling seller and steer federal loan funds to publicly owned systems, threatening the companies' core asset base and ratepayer revenue. A public system owned by its customers does not charge shareholders a return, which is why the industry's interest runs against the bill's public-ownership push.
The bill raises the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 24.5% to fill the trust fund, a broad-based tax on corporate profits that funds water infrastructure the current system does not pay for.

Federally funded water construction would be carried out under project labor agreements where practicable, with prevailing-wage rules preserved, and the bill funds water-operator apprenticeships prioritizing low-income workers.

industries.industry: Water infrastructure engineering and construction firms
industries.note: Tens of billions of dollars a year for pipes, treatment plants, and lead-line replacement would translate directly into contracted work for firms in this sector.
